newsitem.title: FRANCE: French vote, Chirac risks lame-duck presidency.
newsitem.headline: French vote, Chirac risks lame-duck presidency.

text.p: The French voted on Sunday in a knife-edge election which could force Gaullist President Jacques Chirac into tense "cohabitation" with a leftist prime minister and add to doubts over the planned European currency.

The outcome of the runoff ballot was thrown wide open after the Socialist-Communist bloc scored an upset win a week ago in the first round of the parliamentary election following a dull campaign. Voters who abstained in the first round or who backed the far right appeared to hold the key to the result.

Turnout stood at 24.08 percent at midday (1000 GMT), against 17.47 percent at the same time in the 1993 election, the Interior Ministry said. Among key factors in the election is the behaviour of the high proportion of electors -- 31.55 percent -- who stayed away from the polls a week ago.

Polling stations opened at 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) in mainland France and are due to close at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT), when the first results projections will be released. The weather was sunny in most parts but rain was forecast in the south.

Chirac hastily dropped unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe last Monday after his gamble in calling the snap election backfired, and offered voters instead a so-called "dream ticket" of socially conscious Gaullist Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer Alain Madelin.
Seguin, the outgoing National Assembly speaker and only a recent convert to European monetary union, voted early on Sunday morning in his fiefdom of Epinal in eastern France.

If the ruling centre-right coalition loses, Chirac will be forced into "cohabitation" with a hostile government led by Socialist chief Lionel Jospin bent on overturning austerity policies geared to meeting the criteria for the European single currency, or euro.

Jospin has set conditions for joining the euro, including relaxing the Maastricht criteria and gearing the single currency towards creating jobs. The Communists, his possible partners in government, are flatly opposed to joining a single currency.
The centre-right has appealed to voters to think of the future rather than venting short-term irritation at record unemployment and austerity measures needed so that France can qualify for the euro.

In Paris, at a Left Bank market in the Rue Mouffetard, shoppers who last week had ignored electoral matters after a dull campaign were chatting animatedly about Sundays's possible outcome. In a spoof on Tim Burton's zany film "Mars Attacks", stickers had sprouted overnight to warn locals: "Marx attacks: Jospin and (Communist leader Robert) Hue coming soon to a cinema near you."
Juppe, voting in the southwestern city of Bordeaux where he is mayor, told reporters he was living his last hours as prime minister "calmly".
Pollsters said a change in the trend set in the first round would be virtually unprecedented, but was possible if voters stopped thinking of the election as a referendum on Juppe.

"Seguin's last-minute appearance could be seen by voters the same way Margaret Thatcher's replacement by John Major looked to the British, and the far-right supporters may decide to stop the left by backing the centre-right," wrote political analyst Jean-Luc Parodi in the weekly Journal du Dimanche.
"If these conditions come together, then the second round could add yet another surprise to the most surprising election in the Fifth Republic," Parodi wrote.
On the eve of polling, sports fans watching France's rugby union championship final between Toulouse and Bourgoin got an insight into their country's possible political future.

Millions of television viewers saw Chirac sharing the VIP stand with the two men best placed to become his next prime minister. But Jospin was banished to the far end of the front row while Seguin sat at the president's left.
Some 39 million voters were eligible to choose 565 deputies for seats in the 577-strong National Assembly which were not decided in the first round.

National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, whose party took 15 percent of the vote a week ago, urged voters to "punish" the ruling coalition. In 75 constituencies, the Front is pitted against candidates of the centre-right and the leftist bloc.

In the first round, when the combined left polled 40.1 percent of the vote to 36.5 for the centre-right, key candidates in 80 of the 577 constituencies were separated by less than two percentage points.
